data.title: CPI fuels interest rate hike expectations: Crypto market suffers double whammy, nearly 100,000 people liquidated.
data.description:
Author: Zhou, ChainCatcher

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released the August CPI on Friday. Overall prices rose 3.4% year-on-year and 0.4% month-on-month, both figures in line with market expectations. The core CPI, excluding food and energy, slowed to 2.4% year-on-year, the lowest since March 2021, but rose 0.3% month-on-month, higher than the expected 0.2%. Gasoline prices rose 3.9% month-on-month, contributing more than one-third of the overall monthly increase, while the energy index rose 2.1% month-on-month.

In the stock market, before the data release, all Asian markets fell. The Nikkei 225 index closed down 1.93%, the South Korean KOSPI index closed down 1.76%, and the four major A-share indices all opened lower and closed lower.

Following the data release, US stocks opened higher but then declined, ultimately closing higher. The S&P 500 rose 0.9%, while the Dow Jones and Nasdaq both gained approximately 1%, though all three major indices still declined overall for the week. Furthermore, the 10-year US Treasury yield closed at 4.974%, nearing the 5% mark, compared to 4.783% a week earlier. Brent crude oil closed at $104.61 a barrel, up over 8% for the week, with Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities and shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz continuing to push up oil prices. The cryptocurrency market, however, experienced a decline followed by a rise, then a pullback. Bitcoin initially dipped to around $76,000 after the data release, before reaching a high of $79,837. The 50-day moving average briefly crossed above the 200-day moving average on the daily chart, but the price quickly retreated as interest rate hike expectations rose rapidly, rendering the golden cross ineffective on the same day. Ethereum briefly returned above $2,600, showing stronger resilience than Bitcoin. According to Coinglass data, as of press time, total liquidations across the network reached $674 million in the past 24 hours, affecting approximately 94,000 investors. Ethereum saw the largest liquidations at $311 million, followed by Bitcoin at $184 million. The largest single liquidation occurred in an ETH-USD position on Hyperliquid, amounting to approximately $20.28 million.

Rate hike probability rises to 80%, Fed decision next week remains uncertain

For the Fed, the weight of the August CPI data was already elevated before its release. Bank of America analysts previously stated that the August non-farm payrolls were more like an appetizer, and the main course that would truly determine the direction of the September 15-16 interest rate meeting was still the CPI. The bank believes that unless there is a significant unexpected decline in employment data, non-farm payrolls are unlikely to be the final deciding factor in whether or not to raise interest rates, and maintains its judgment of a September rate hike. The subsequent release of August's non-farm payrolls, showing an increase of 162,000 jobs, roughly three times the expected figure, had already pushed the discussion of interest rate hikes a step further. Following the release of the CPI data, market sentiment regarding next week's Federal Reserve interest rate meeting clearly shifted towards a hawkish stance. The latest data from Polymarket shows that the market is betting an 80% probability of a 25 basis point rate hike by the Fed on September 16th, a 21% probability of keeping rates unchanged, and about a 1% probability of a rate hike of more than 50 basis points. The probability of any rate cut is less than 1%. Before the CPI release, keeping rates unchanged was the most probable option for a considerable period, only being quickly overtaken by the rate hike option around the time of the data release.

CICC Research points out that the August CPI has already reached the threshold for a Fed rate hike, and a 25 basis point rate hike is expected on September 16th. The Fed may also lower its unemployment rate forecast and raise its inflation forecast, signaling a tightening. The financial blog Zero Hedge emphasizes that core CPI is overheated, and super core inflation is even hotter, with education and communication service prices experiencing historic increases, including a record surge in mobile communication service prices.

Goldman Sachs economist Alexandra Wilson-Elizondo stated that while the day's CPI superficially met investors' expectations, it increased the suspense surrounding next week's interest rate decision.

She believes the data does not fully reflect some of the recent inflationary pressures, and there is almost no evidence that inflation will return to target in the short term. Energy remains an exogenous variable in this logic. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities, shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi Arabia's closure of the East-West oil pipeline continue to fuel supply concerns. The coexistence of high oil prices and high interest rates has led Wall Street to rewrite the question as how long high interest rates will last and whether policies can suppress inflation without significantly harming the economy and corporate profits. RBC Capital Markets has revised its outlook for this year from previous expectations of rate cuts to three rate hikes, believing that high interest rates may further suppress corporate profits and stock valuations. Nick Timiraos, a Fed mouthpiece, recently wrote that investors have largely accepted that the Fed will raise rates for the first time in three years next week; the more difficult question is what will happen afterward. Almost no one within the Federal Reserve believes that a single 25-basis-point rate hike is sufficient to suppress inflation. If a rate hike is chosen next week, most investors will interpret it as a correction of previous interest rate levels, suggesting a one-time increase is unlikely. Since the 1990s, the Fed has rarely stopped after just one rate hike. Warsh stated in July that he doesn't believe the Fed is adept at fine-tuning. Analysts judge that a chairman skeptical of fine-tuning is unlikely to declare the job done after a 25-basis-point rate hike. The market currently expects at least three rate hikes by June next year, higher than the previous expectation of two. For risk assets, Friday's rebound mainly stemmed from a clearer policy path; inflationary pressures themselves have not truly subsided. Reduced policy uncertainty explains why US stocks still closed higher despite rising rate hike expectations. The real pricing point is still at the September 16th decision, dot plot, and Warsh's press conference. The Bitcoin golden cross was a one-day wonder, with resistance emerging at $82,000. The crypto market reacted even more violently to this data. In the four hours following the CPI release, Bitcoin first dipped to $76,000, then rebounded to break through $79,000, before falling back to around $77,600. According to Coinglass data, $471 million in positions were liquidated across the network in those four hours, including $348 million in short positions and $123 million in long positions, a typical double whammy for both long and short positions. Renowned trader Killa published statistics pointing out that after the past three US CPI releases, Bitcoin rose by more than 5% within eight days. He believes the market has already priced in the negative news, and a bear market trap has been set. Looking at a longer timeframe, the crypto market has seen significant volatility recently. According to Coinglass data, Bitcoin rose 24.95% in August, its best monthly performance this year, but its momentum weakened in September, falling 1.83% within the month. In terms of fund flows, Bitcoin and Ethereum spot ETFs have diverged. According to SoSoValue data, the Bitcoin spot ETF saw a net outflow of $463 million this week, with net assets of approximately $97.58 billion, corresponding to a Bitcoin price of approximately $77,286; the Ethereum spot ETF saw a net inflow of $197 million during the same period, with net assets of approximately $16.31 billion, corresponding to a price of approximately $2,539.

Regarding listed treasury companies, according to SoSoValue data, as of September 8th, Eastern Time, the scale of global listed companies increasing their Bitcoin holdings slowed significantly last week. Excluding mining companies, the net purchase total was $267 million, a 48% decrease from the previous week.

The total holdings of listed companies amounted to 1,119,973 Bitcoins, a 2.38% decrease from the previous week, with a market capitalization of approximately $87.77 billion, representing 5.6% of Bitcoin's circulating market capitalization. Strategy's most recent increase in holdings occurred on August 31st, purchasing 4,600 Bitcoins, bringing its total holdings to 845,050 Bitcoins, currently showing a slight unrealized profit. According to Strategy's latest 8-K filing, the company has raised approximately $20.9 billion this year, ranking fourth in US stock offerings, behind only SpaceX, Alphabet, and Intel. In contrast, Ethereum treasury company Bitmine continues to increase its holdings against the trend, adding 28,086 Ethereum last week, bringing its total holdings to 5,929,200 Bitcoins, with an average cost of $3,347, resulting in an unrealized loss of approximately $5 billion at the current price. From a technical perspective, on September 12th, Bitcoin briefly rose to $79,837, with the 50-day moving average briefly crossing above the 200-day moving average on the daily chart. The price then retreated, and the golden cross disappeared. This was the first daily golden cross Bitcoin had seen since November 2025, and also the fastest to fail, indicating a simultaneous cooling of short-term momentum. Similar golden crosses that appeared in 2021, February 2023, October 2024, and May 2025 were followed by a pullback, suggesting the golden cross is more of a lagging signal, often appearing after a significant portion of the upward movement has already occurred. Regarding on-chain tokens, analyst Murphy pointed out that short-term holders' tokens are mainly distributed in the $59,000 to $81,000 range. A break above $82,000 would mean that all these positions are now profitable, creating an incentive for short-term funds to cash out. The highest concentration of long-term holders' holdings is between $81,000 and $82,000, including many who were passively held after being trapped in a losing position and are likely to exit when the price approaches their cost basis. Whales holding more than 100,000 tokens are concentrated in two areas around $40,000, with the rest accumulating between $78,000 and $82,000. Glassnode states that Bitcoin is currently constrained by supply pressure from long-term holders around $83,000 to $85,000. If it breaks below this newly formed concentration zone, $75,000 will become a key level to watch, and further declines could lead to a return to the accumulation platform around $60,000. CryptoQuant analyst Axel Adler Jr. points out that the proportion of Bitcoin supply in a profitable state has rebounded from about 47% at the end of June to about 69%, and the 90-day change has also quickly turned positive from -19% in early August to about 41%, which is one of the fastest recoverys in Bitcoin's history.

Next week's regulatory calendar overlaps with the interest rate meeting. Zach Pandl, head of research at Grayscale, stated that the US CLARITY bill, which aims to establish comprehensive rules for the crypto market, will face a procedural vote in the Senate on September 15th, requiring 60 votes. Republicans currently hold 53 seats, and progress still requires Democratic cooperation. Even if the bill fails to pass this year, the regulatory framework for areas such as stablecoins, token issuance, tokenized securities, and perpetual futures will continue to become clearer.

... Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong pointed out that reaching $400,000 for Bitcoin by 2030 remains a reasonable target, and he personally believes the bottom of this cycle may have already been reached. He also stated that regardless of the vote result on September 15th, the SEC and CFTC are prepared to advance rules based on their existing authority, and the industry may still gain new regulatory clarity before and after the vote.

data.title: Crypto Newcomers' Gold Rush: Coinbase's Co-creation Adventure in Venezuelan Oil Fields
data.description:
Author: Zen, PANews

After making enough money in the crypto industry, where should the next investment go? Coinbase co-founder Fred Ehrsam recently gave a surprising answer: oil fields. This 38-year-old crypto billionaire has been frequently seen in Caracas, the capital of Venezuela, over the past few months, and has even stayed in local hotels for extended periods.

After months of travel, in early September, Fred Ehrsam finally reaped his first "harvest." Primavera Infinita, which he co-founded, officially signed a production participation contract with Venezuela's state-owned oil company PDVSA, gaining the opportunity to develop the Buare-Elotes block oil field. PDVSA's long-term goal is for the block to contribute more than 70,000 barrels per day of new production.

This is also an investment that is hard to reconcile with Ehrsam's resume.

He previously worked as a forex trader at Goldman Sachs, co-founded Coinbase with Brian Armstrong in 2012, and co-founded the crypto investment firm Paradigm in 2018. His investment portfolio later expanded to include cutting-edge technology companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX. Why would someone who has accumulated wealth through digital assets and invested in software and cutting-edge technology for the long term choose to venture into politically risky Venezuela to compete for a traditional resource that humans have been exploiting for over a century? Perhaps the answer lies not only in oil. While established oil giants hesitated, Ehrsam rushed in. Looking solely at its oil resources, Venezuela is a place that cannot be ignored. However, over the past two decades, the country's vast underground resources have not translated into commensurate production. In the late 1990s, Venezuela's daily crude oil production once reached approximately 3 million barrels; today, it is only 1.25 million barrels per day. Long-term sanctions, insufficient investment, aging equipment, coupled with political and property rights risks, have gradually made Venezuela, a country possessing one of the world's largest proven oil reserves, a unique entity in the global oil industry. The oil reserves are not lacking; what is truly lacking is sustained capital investment, well-maintained infrastructure, and a continuous loss of technical talent and operational capabilities. However, starting in 2026, the situation changed. After Maduro's arrest by the US and Delcy Rodríguez's appointment as interim president, relations between the US and Venezuela were rapidly restructured. Specifically in the oil industry, Venezuela reformed its oil laws, allowing more private capital to participate in production under new models; the Trump administration placed oil at the core of its Venezuelan strategy, pushing for sanctions and contract framework adjustments while urging US energy companies to invest approximately $100 billion locally. This has made Venezuela's oil industry a market undergoing a repricing process. A country long avoided by global capital due to years of sanctions and economic crisis could potentially offer returns far exceeding those of mature markets once it reopens. Judging from his subsequent choices, Ehrsam is clearly willing to take the risk for this potential return. He co-founded Primavera earlier this year with Manuel Iribarren, a Venezuelan graduate of Stanford. In February, the two arrived in Venezuela to seek investment opportunities. After meetings with Venezuelan leaders and PdVSA executives, they were most interested in high-risk investments like oil and gas. This is actually a familiar odds structure for VCs, and what attracted Ehrsam the most. It's not about finding a 10% undervaluation in a stable, transparent market, but rather about accepting a huge probability of failure in a place where many investors dare not enter, in exchange for significant asset revaluation potential after institutional changes. However, this potentially high-return water is extremely deep, and not everyone is willing to wade in. In fact, Trump had urged companies like ExxonMobil, ConocoPhillips, and Continental Resources (owned by oil tycoon Harold Hamm) to invest $100 billion, but these established energy giants remained hesitant. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, which had deep roots in Venezuela, experienced the nationalization of assets during the Chavez era. This legacy of claims makes them more sensitive to issues such as property rights, arbitration, and whether the next government will continue to recognize current contracts. Of course, not all oil giants are so hesitant. Chevron, which has operated in Venezuela for decades, announced in early September that it would invest $7 billion in Venezuelan oil fields over the next five years, hoping to increase its production in Venezuela to approximately 600,000 barrels per day. Sources familiar with the matter revealed that the terms of the new joint venture contract between Chevron and PdVSA are expected to be very favorable, which is believed to reduce the risk of further investment in the country.

“Disorderly land grabbing benefits no one”

In this round of Venezuelan oil liberalization, in addition to established energy companies like Chevron, a number of smaller, riskier independent oil and gas companies and new capital have also emerged. They come from diverse backgrounds, but share a striking commonality—various degrees of connection with Trump and his political network.

Ehrsam rarely mentions his political views publicly, but according to federal fundraising records, he donated $1 million to the Trump-Vance Inauguration Committee, establishing connections with the Trump administration and currently serving on the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. For an oil project highly dependent on US sanctions policies, Venezuelan domestic law, and the direction of bilateral relations, this political access is itself a valuable resource.

It can significantly reduce information asymmetry and change investors' assessment of the risk of policy reversal. Similar connections have also emerged with other new entrants. Denver-based Aspect Holdings has signed a contract with Venezuela's state-owned oil company, PdVSA, to participate in local technology research. Aspect is a private energy investment and exploration firm founded by billionaire Alex Cranberg, a long-time major Republican donor. Another company attempting to enter the Venezuelan market, Sable Offshore, is led by oil industry veteran Jim Flores. Sable has a more traditional energy industry background, but it also has noteworthy policy overlaps with the Trump administration. Previously, when California regulators opposed its resumption of offshore oil production in Santa Barbara, Sable ultimately secured federal support through an executive order signed by Trump, allowing the project to proceed. A more typical example is Dallas-based Hunt Oil. On August 18, the company signed a production participation contract with Venezuela to participate in the development and production increase of the Caro and Carisito oil and gas fields in the east. Hunt Oil is not a new player in the oil industry, but an independent energy company with decades of experience in oil and gas development. The Hunt family behind it is a long-time supporter of Trump and the Republican Party. However, rather than saying the Trump administration is "allocating" Venezuelan oil fields, it's more accurate to say that these American capital firms are more willing to believe the current policy window will continue and are more willing to bear the resulting tail risks. Conversely, for established giants like ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips, their continued hesitation is not due to unfamiliarity with Venezuela, but rather because they are too familiar with it. Precisely because they have experienced the nationalization of assets, lengthy arbitrations, and repeated sanctions, they are more cautious about the stability of property rights and the continuity of policies. This contrast has also raised concerns within Venezuela's oil industry. Some veterans question whether these new entrants possess sufficient capital and expertise to handle Venezuela's complex heavy oil projects. Local crude oil has high viscosity, infrastructure is aging, and development and transportation require continuous investment; moreover, Venezuela's massive debt may make banks cautious about project financing, ultimately forcing many investments to rely more heavily on equity investors. Pedro Burelli, a Venezuelan opposition figure and former director of PdVSA, believes that oil fields should be handed over to companies with sufficient capital and experience in complex projects, rather than being rapidly divided up after the policy window opens. Burelli stated that the current disorderly land grab benefits no one. Betting on the Open Political Window The question arises: what should an investor like Fred Ehrsam, who has never been involved in the oil industry and is now venturing into the most complex Venezuelan market, do? The most familiar approach in venture capital is to first find undervalued assets or entrepreneurs, and then solve subsequent problems by recruiting a management team, raising additional funding, and integrating resources. Ehrsam is clearly trying to replicate this approach. Lacking experience in the oil and gas industry, he has brought in a professional team including seasoned oil expert Dheeraj Verma. However, the difference between oil fields and software companies is not simply a matter of "asset-heavy" versus "asset-light." What truly differentiates them is the method of capital investment and the payback period. For a software company, once funds are received, they can be quickly converted into team expansion and market growth. If growth falls short of expectations, losses can be mitigated through layoffs, reduced investment, product adjustments, or even business transformation. While many costs are also significant, new investments are often easier to phase out, reduce, or reallocate. The logic in the oil industry is entirely different. Whether it's well repair, pipeline construction, equipment upgrades, or improvements to storage and transportation systems, substantial upfront capital investment is required before production is realized. Moreover, a significant portion of these investments is highly irreversible; a project's profitability depends on its ability to continue production, exports, and settlements over the next few years, ultimately recouping the initial investment. For Ehrsam and his Primavera, the biggest risk may not stem from oil technology itself, but rather from the mismatch between the payback period and the political cycle. Oilfield projects may take years to reach a stable return, but US sanctions against Venezuela, local oil laws, the contract enforcement environment, and bilateral relations could all change during this period. It's worth noting that Chevron's investment even includes international arbitration rights in the new terms. This precisely illustrates that what established oil companies are truly concerned about is whether the contracts will still be valid five or ten years after investing billions of dollars. Because whether a contract signed today will be executed under the same conditions five years from now is something no one can guarantee. This is also why other traditional oil giants are particularly cautious about Venezuela. From this perspective, Ehrsam's real bet isn't just on how much more production the Budare-Elotes block can generate, but on how long this current political window will remain open. The new money of the digital age is ultimately returning to the most traditional assets. Leaving aside Ehrsam's bet on the Venezuelan political climate, investing in the traditional energy sector is a phenomenon worth observing in the cryptocurrency industry. If we only look at Primavera, this can still be understood as a personal adventure by a crypto billionaire. But by broadening our perspective beyond Ehrsam, we find that similar asset preferences are not entirely isolated. In February of this year, BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes unusually publicly disclosed his asset allocation. In addition to cryptocurrencies such as BTC, ETH, ZEC, and HYPE, his stock portfolio covers gold, silver, copper, and uranium miners, major oil companies, Latin American energy companies, and defense companies, while also directly holding physical gold. This asset allocation has revealed a significant shift: for someone accumulating wealth through cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin is not an exclusive asset compared to gold, copper, uranium, and oil; rather, they appear together on the same balance sheet. Tether, with annual profits in the tens of billions of dollars, has gone even further in this regard. In 2025, the USDT issuer's net profit exceeded $10 billion. By the end of that year, the company stated that its independent investment portfolio, built using its profits and excess capital, exceeded $20 billion, covering multiple industries including AI, energy, precious metals, agriculture, land, and communications. One of Tether's most notable investments also occurred in South America. In 2024, Tether first acquired approximately 9.8% of the agricultural group Adecoagro for $100 million; in 2025, it launched a cash tender offer, ultimately increasing its stake to 70%. The latter offer alone involved 49.597 million shares at $12.41 per share, corresponding to approximately $615 million in cash expenditure. Tether's acquisition of a controlling stake in Adecoagro wasn't about putting it on-chain and packaging it as an RWA agricultural project; rather, it involved a traditional company that genuinely owns land, farms, processing plants, and power generation facilities. Adecoagro manages over 200,000 hectares of sugarcane plantations in Brazil, owns three sugar mills producing sugar, ethanol, and electricity; and also operates rice and dairy businesses in Argentina and Uruguay. Its sugar mills can utilize sugarcane waste for combined heat and power (CHP), selling surplus electricity to the local grid after meeting its own energy needs. This even creates a rather interesting inversion. For the past few years, the crypto industry has been talking about "real-world assets," exploring how to bring real-world assets onto the blockchain. Tether's transaction, however, followed a different path. Instead of first packaging agricultural assets into tokens, it directly acquired control of an agricultural and energy production company. From this perspective, Hayes, Tether, and Ehrsam actually represent three different paths: gaining exposure to resource prices through stocks, directly acquiring control of physical production companies, and directly participating in oil field operations. These are not strictly progressive, but they collectively illustrate that crypto capital's interest in real-world assets has moved beyond simply "how to put assets on-chain" and is beginning to manifest in more traditional holding and operating methods. In fact, the flow of funds to energy, metals, and land is not entirely accidental. These assets possess a scarcity entirely different from crypto assets. Bitcoin's 21 million-coin cap is written in the code, while the supply constraints of oil fields, mines, and land are written in geology, geography, and long development cycles. The former is a man-made but highly reliable digital scarcity, while the latter is a physical scarcity that is difficult to change in the short term through capital and technology. Fred Ehrsam's Venezuelan adventure is just one of the most extreme examples. Starting with a wealth system almost entirely composed of code and networks, he ultimately staked his hard-earned money in oil fields that required years of investment, were impossible to move, and whose fate was simultaneously determined by geology and politics. Crypto can create and transfer wealth very quickly, but when a portion of that wealth begins to seek a longer-term, larger-scale destination, it ultimately seeks its final anchor in physical entities whose networks cannot be disconnected.

data.title: What criminal risks should AI entrepreneurs be aware of when going global? Analysis of 5 popular sectors.
data.description:
Author: Lawyer Shao Shiwei

From a macro perspective, AI exports are experiencing a period of rapid growth. In the first half of 2026, China's AI-related product exports accounted for 22.7% of total exports, contributing 8.6 percentage points to overall export growth. AI going global is already an industry consensus.

However, for AI entrepreneurs, going global doesn't mean they only need to consider overseas markets and local regulations.

On September 7, 2026, the Supreme People's Court issued the "Opinions on Legally Handling Disputes Involving Artificial Intelligence," explicitly including acts such as using artificial intelligence to commit fraud, infringe on citizens' personal information, and produce and disseminate obscene materials within the scope of criminal prosecution.

In the same month, the first case in China involving AI going overseas and being involved in pornography was publicly sentenced (➡️《"Breaking the AI ​​Model to Profit from Pornography? Court: It Constitutes the Crime of Producing Obscene Materials for Profit!") - Developer Zheng was once an AI programmer at a major domestic game company. His "OchatAi_bot" chatbot was launched on an overseas platform in January 2025. After discovering illegal clues, the public security organs arrested all the people involved in the case within two months. The Yuyao Court of Zhejiang Province sentenced six people to more than three years in prison for the crime of producing obscene materials for profit.

(Software involved in the case)

This article aims to discuss: Facing the industry trend and market opportunities of AI going global, where exactly is the boundary between growth and compliance for AI entrepreneurs?

1. Why are more and more AI entrepreneurs choosing to go global?

In the past, when discussing going global, the logic was often "the domestic market is too competitive, so we go overseas to find growth." But now the driving forces behind AI going global are more complex.

On the one hand, there is a supply mismatch.

Many AI application categories that have already been successfully implemented overseas—video translation, e-commerce product image generation, automated changelog—either lack comparable products in China or are not well-developed. Using proven scenarios to serve the global market has a higher success rate than competing in the red ocean of China. On the other hand, there is a difference in payment structure. IDC data shows that hardware accounts for as much as 74.3% of AI spending in China, while hardware accounts for only 18.0% in Latin America, and software accounts for 60.9%[1]. Overseas markets are more willing to pay for software and solutions rather than buying servers and computing cards. This is a clear entry point for Chinese teams that are good at application layer development. Simply put, the advantages of Chinese AI entrepreneurs are: lower model and computing power costs, proven application scenarios, and small and fast full-stack teams. These advantages point to overseas expansion directions that are mostly concentrated in a few tracks: AI companion social networking, digital humans, AI marketing, AI stock trading, and AI Agent. These sectors have genuine market demand and mature overseas counterparts. However, after product launch, as pressure from user needs, paid conversions, and revenue growth increases, some originally normal product features may be pushed further forward, gradually entering high-risk legal territory. Often, entrepreneurs don't intentionally break the law; rather, the boundaries slowly change through repeated product iterations and business choices. 2. The Evolution of Risks in Popular AI Sectors: Where Did They Go Wrong? Few entrepreneurs in the AI ​​sector initially intend to create illegal products. A more common path is: the team discovers that a certain type of user need has higher retention and a stronger willingness to pay, so they continuously optimize the product around these needs—until the product's core selling point itself crosses legal boundaries. The following analysis, using specific cases, examines the risk evolution paths of several typical sectors.

1. AI Companionship/Social Interaction: From Emotional Value to Paid Pornographic Content

AI companionship is a real and rapidly growing sector. The initial products focused on emotional companionship and role-playing in romantic scenarios. However, after a period of operation, teams discovered a very real data pattern: ordinary chat users would leave after a few conversations, while romantic interaction users had higher retention rates. Furthermore, as the level of explicit dialogue increased, chat duration, points consumption, and recharge rates rose significantly.

At this point, companies faced a business decision: since the more explicit the content, the more profitable it was, should it be made a core selling point? Thus, they began adding more explicit character cards, adjusting system prompts to optimize pornographic dialogue capabilities, and adding image and video generation to higher-level paid packages. The product progressed step by step along the path of "AI companionship → romantic simulation → pornographic chat → paid generation of obscene content."

The first case of domestic AI going overseas involving pornography, mentioned at the beginning of this article, is a typical example.

Developer Zheng's initial motivation was the market opportunity in the AI ​​companionship sector, but the final product evolution led the entire team into the realm of criminal law. Similarly, if AI dating products begin using algorithms to identify users' willingness to pay, shifting the matching results from "dating" to "paid companionship" or even facilitating offline special services, the risk path follows the same logic. Lawyer Shao advises: The real point where risk escalates is not when a user makes an inappropriate request, but when the company begins to proactively optimize its product and design growth strategies around high-risk demands. 2. AI Marketing: From Automated Customer Acquisition to Automated Fraud Infrastructure The core value of AI in marketing is reducing the cost of large-scale personalized communication. However, the same capabilities—mass-generating personas, automating private messaging, customizing scripts based on user profiles, and continuously cultivating trust—become a fraudulent assembly line when used for fraud conversion. In July 2026, OpenAI publicly disclosed that it had blocked a fraud network based in Poipet, Cambodia [2]. The network used ChatGPT to translate messages, generate social media content, and build fake identities to carry out investment fraud and romance fraud according to the standard process of "contact - induce emotions - harvest money". What AI does here is to scale up the whole process of "account nurturing - chat - build trust - conversion" that originally required a lot of manual work. For entrepreneurs of AI marketing SaaS, the dangerous evolution path is: ordinary AI copywriting tools are highly competitive and not expensive, but if the product can register accounts in batches, automatically generate personas, maintain relationships through long-term chat, and accurately convert, some customers are willing to pay much higher prices. In order to continuously add functions such as fake identities, batch account nurturing, and emotional inducement for these indicators, the product may change from a "marketing tool" to the infrastructure of illegal business. Attorney Shao's Tip: The features clients are most willing to pay for may be the high-risk product features. When a team starts differentiating itself around these features, company leaders and product managers need to further assess: Is this feature feasible, and should it be implemented? 3. AI Stock Trading: From Assisted Analysis to Trading for Users AI as an auxiliary investment analysis tool is a normal direction for fintech; however, once AI directly provides users with stock buying and selling advice or specific investment conclusions, it is no longer a "normal product direction," but rather a securities investment consulting business that requires a license. In September 2026, the Supreme People's Procuratorate released typical cases of technical support for intellectual property prosecution cases, including the "DIY Stock Trading Robot" case tried by the Jing'an District Court of Shanghai. (➡️Are AI stock trading software illegal? Are programmers breaking the law by developing such products? Analysis of a real case in Shanghai). This company initially developed stock quantitative SaaS software. Due to the lack of securities qualifications, early users could only perform data analysis and simulated trading; actual trading had to be done on the brokerage platform, resulting in very few users. To overcome its operational difficulties, the company began to add more direct trading capabilities—the product could later automatically buy and sell stocks based on preset conditions, and it bypassed the technical protection measures of the brokerage trading system by purchasing a program to achieve integration. Ultimately, the actual controller was sentenced to seven years and nine months in prison for illegal business operations and copyright infringement. In September 2026, this case was selected by the Supreme People's Procuratorate as a typical case of technical support for intellectual property prosecution. Lawyer Shao's advice: From tools to services, from analysis to decision-making, from assistance to replacement, each step may trigger different regulatory qualification requirements. 4. AI Digital Humans and AI Agents: The Stronger the Technology, the Greater the Risk Exposure What legal risks might AI digital humans face when used for face-swapping, voice-changing, and impersonating real people? AI digital humans have a wide range of normal applications—live-streaming e-commerce, corporate training, and short video production—but the same technology used for face-swapping, voice-changing, and generating false identity content carries criminal risks. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security jointly shut down two deepfake websites and coordinated with law enforcement agencies in France and Italy. This shows that some applications are not as simple as AI entrepreneurs and developers mistakenly believe: "They can't be done domestically, but they're fine overseas." Where are the boundaries for AI agents acquiring user data, account keys, and third-party system permissions? Regarding AI Agents, when "fully automated" becomes a core selling point, teams continuously grant the Agent more permissions: reading more data, saving login status, and cross-platform operation. The greater the permissions, the better the product experience, and the more willing users are to pay—but once the Agent's permission design crosses the legal boundaries of data security and computer crime, it may constitute a crime of infringing on citizens' personal information or illegally obtaining data from computer information systems. The Cyberspace Administration of China's normative document released in April this year directly points out the risk scenario of "using intelligent agent technology to steal user data or account keys." Attorney Shao advises: The common characteristic of these two tracks is that improvements in technical indicators (more realistic, more autonomous) and increases in legal risks often go in the same direction. When teams pursue "more lifelike" and "more automated" as product competitiveness, they need to simultaneously assess whether each technological upgrade has crossed into an area requiring compliance review.

3 How can AI entrepreneurs control criminal risks in the early stages of product growth?

Reviewing the above cases, we can see that AI entrepreneurs did not initially intend to create illegal products. The developers in the Yuyao case saw a market opportunity in the AI ​​companion sector, while the founder of the "DIY stock trading robot" initially created a compliant quantitative analysis tool. What truly led the product into the criminal risk zone were seemingly reasonable product decisions made under growth pressure—each step, individually, was about "optimizing customer experience" and "improving conversion rates," but accumulated, the nature of the product fundamentally changed.

This means that compliance work for AI going global cannot wait until product problems arise. Entrepreneurs need to establish several basic checks early in product design and growth decisions:

First, identify how far your product is from the legal red line. Some sectors are naturally closer to risk—products involving content generation, financial transactions, identity simulation, and data collection should have clear boundaries set from day one.

Second, be wary of the "most profitable feature." When a team discovers that a certain type of demand or feature has brought far higher-than-expected paid conversion rates and retention rates, it's precisely at this point that they should stop and examine: Is this growth driver itself compliant? Third, don't assume that "going overseas exempts you from domestic law." The first case of AI-related pornography overseas has proven that AI products operated by Chinese citizens on overseas platforms are also subject to domestic criminal law. For entrepreneurs, opportunities and risks often follow the same path. Making trade-offs between conversion efficiency and compliance boundaries is a challenge every AI entrepreneur must face from day one of product development. Audiences will naturally place more trust in creators with verifiable track records, although track records are by no means the sole criterion—just as the most popular chess creators (GothamChess and the Botez sisters) are not the most skilled chess masters, but they are the best at telling chess stories (this principle also applies to the entire esports content field). My advice: Put away your arrogance and prejudice. Stop criticizing the public offering and trading of Meme Coin, and don't belittle those young creators with curly hair. data.title: Refuting Ethereum's claim of "abandoning" ETH: What does it mean to pay gas without using ETH?
data.description:
Author: imToken

If you're involved in on-chain transactions, you've likely encountered these awkward situations:

Received stablecoins in a new address, but when trying to transfer them out, a pop-up window popped up saying there was no ETH to pay the gas; wanted to exchange coins on a DEX but got stuck; withdrew USDC from a trading platform only to realize you hadn't prepared the gas.....

All of these situations force you to find fiat currency channels elsewhere or beg others to transfer some "water" (equity), which is arguably the most classic scene of discouraging newcomers in the crypto world.

Recently, Vitalik Buterin mentioned the progress of EIP-8141 (Frame Transactions), once again bringing new possibilities to the forefront: in the future, even without ETH in your wallet, you can directly transfer funds, and the gas can be deducted directly from USDC. Some applications, in order to attract users, might even simply cover your gas.

The news quickly escalated into a alarming claim: "If we don't need ETH to use Ethereum anymore, what value will ETH have?" The answer isn't that simple. What users use to pay fees and what the Ethereum protocol ultimately uses to settle fees are two completely different things. First, what does it mean to not use ETH to pay gas? Let's start with a typical Ethereum transaction today. For example, Frank has 1000 USDC in his wallet and wants to transfer 100 USDC to a friend, but if he doesn't have ETH in his wallet, the transaction cannot be sent. The reason is simple: the current logic of ordinary Ethereum accounts is very rigid. The person initiating the transaction is also responsible for paying the network gas—Frank's signature, Frank's initiation of the transaction, and Frank's ETH balance paying the gas are essentially tied together. EIP-8141 aims to break these three things down. According to the current design, a Frame Transaction can be broken down into multiple different "Frames," each responsible for verifying the transaction, confirming who pays the gas, and actually executing the user's action. Therefore, in the future, when Frank makes a transfer, he can still sign to prove "this 100 USDC is indeed what I want to transfer," but another Paymaster or account will use ETH to pay the gas to the Ethereum network on Frank's behalf, and Frank will then use a small amount of USDC to pay the fee to this Paymaster. For Frank, all he might see is a transfer of 100 USDC and a network fee of 0.1 USDC. Throughout the process, he doesn't even need to know the ETH gas cost or prepare ETH beforehand. However, from the Ethereum protocol's perspective, it doesn't mean "Ethereum starts accepting USDC as gas." It simply means someone in the background pays Frank's gas with ETH and then settles the payment with him in USDC. The official ERC-20 payment example provided by EIP-8141 uses a similar structure. The Sponsor is responsible for approval and bears the gas, while users transfer ERC-20 tokens to the Sponsor as payment. This is easier to understand if compared to real-life consumption. When we use a RMB credit card in Japan, the user perceives a "RMB deduction," while the merchant may receive Japanese Yen. However, this doesn't mean the underlying settlement currency in Japan has become RMB. The front-end payment asset and the back-end settlement asset can be different things.

EIP-8141 essentially does a similar abstraction. Ultimately, users no longer need to hold ETH themselves; other accounts can pay the ETH gas on their behalf, and then use assets such as USDC to complete the fee settlement.

The two may seem to differ by only a few words, but their meanings for ETH are completely different.

II. Why does Ethereum insist on "hiding" the gas?

In fact, "not needing to prepare ETH yourself" is not a completely new idea. ERC-4337's introduction of Account Abstraction and Paymaster already allows smart accounts to implement Gas Sponsorship, enabling applications to pay transaction fees on behalf of users or allowing users to bear the fees using stablecoins. However, while ERC-4337 can do this, it primarily adds a separate infrastructure of UserOperation, Bundler, EntryPoint, and Paymaster outside the protocol. EIP-8141, on the other hand, attempts to integrate these capabilities more natively into the Ethereum transaction structure itself. Ultimately, the core issue is to solve a problem that should have been addressed long ago: why should ordinary users need to understand what Gas is? In real life, if you transfer 200 yuan to a friend via WeChat, WeChat will never pop up a window asking you to "buy 2 yuan worth of clearing tokens from another platform first." But crypto has always been this frustrating. On Ethereum, you need to prepare ETH; on Solana, you need to exchange for SOL; on the BNB Chain, you need to accumulate BNB. Even when switching to a new L2 blockchain, the first reaction is to check if you have enough initial capital in your wallet. Experienced users might be able to handle this in two minutes by crossing chains, but for outsiders, it's a formidable barrier that can make them immediately close the webpage and leave. Besides hiding gas fees, frame transactions can also solve many other persistent problems. For example, when trading a new token on a DEX, you have to click "Approve" to authorize, then "Swap," and confirm twice via wallet pop-ups. If the latter "Swap" fails, the former authorization remains on the chain for a long time, leaving the risk of theft. If we use Frames, these two things can be packaged into an atomic batch: if the swap fails, the previous authorizations are automatically rolled back cleanly. This involves a much larger scope for imagination; who will authorize, who will execute, who will pay, and what verification methods will be used can all be broken down and recombined. Third, is this good or bad news for ETH? This is also the area where this discussion is most likely to go to two extremes. One argument is, "If you don't need to use ETH to pay gas in the future, ETH will have no value," while another argument is, "Lowering the user threshold and causing a surge in transaction volume is a huge boon for ETH." Regarding major architectural changes affecting the user experience of the underlying protocol, it's still difficult to draw definitive conclusions. However, one thing is certain: EIP-8141 has not eliminated ETH's role as the underlying gas and fee settlement asset for Ethereum. Users may not be aware of ETH, but Paymaster, applications, or other accounts responsible for paying on behalf of users still need to be able to handle network fees denominated in ETH. The existing EIP-1559 fee market has not been replaced by stablecoins due to Frames. What has changed is the position of ETH demand. Today, there might be a million users, each keeping a small amount of ETH in their wallets for gas payments; in the future, it might become a small number of Paymasters, wallet service providers, and applications holding larger ETH balances, then handling gas payments for a large number of ordinary users. Of course, don't naively assume that "every time a user pays in stablecoins, the backend will buy the equivalent amount of ETH at market price on the secondary market." Payment intermediaries have their own inventory management and hedging strategies, making it difficult to directly translate into the instant buying power that retail investors fantasize about. Paymaster can prepare inventory in advance, replenish its reserves dynamically, and use other fund management methods. Therefore, it's difficult to directly deduce the magnitude of new ETH buying simply because "stablecoins can be used to pay gas in the future." The real key to success lies in one thing: Does the improved user experience ultimately lead to more real demand for Ethereum, and can it actually increase the overall market size? Let's do the math: If in the past 100 people planned to enter the market, and 70 of them were bogged down by gas purchases, Gwei calculations, and cross-chain issues, ultimately only 30 people completed their transactions; If in the future wallets handle all these hassles in the background, allowing 80 people to smoothly complete their transactions—even if they don't have a single ETH—the actual ETH consumed and destroyed by the network will be far greater than before; Conversely, if the entire ecosystem doesn't bring any incremental activity and merely replaces "paying out of pocket" with "having someone else pay," then it certainly won't generate any new incremental value.

In conclusion

From the author's perspective, it weakens the requirement that "every user must accumulate some ETH in advance to use Ethereum," but it bets that once this barrier disappears, more people will actually start using Ethereum.

For ordinary users, there's certainly no need to change their usage habits because of this EIP, but from the perspective of wallet development, the direction it points to is already very clear.

A truly user-friendly wallet in the future will likely require users to understand gas fees beforehand. Users will be responsible for deciding where their assets will go and what operations they will perform; the wallet will inform them of the risks and the final cost. The complex protocol details—which account to use for payment, whether to use ETH or stablecoins for billing, and whether available gas sponsors—should gradually be hidden in the background. Truly mature infrastructure often operates in this manner.

The new bill adds regulatory provisions for "non-decentralized finance (DeFi) trading protocols." Such protocols must be registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), with the CFTC and the US Treasury Department developing supporting rules. The new text does not contain major changes to the ethical provisions, and the Department of Justice remains responsible for enforcing the relevant regulations, while Democrats had previously demanded that state attorneys general be given more enforcement powers.
